project.name: opensourcedating
project.tagline: An open-source dating app, piloted in Berlin. One accountable server first, a network of vetted servers later. Chats are end-to-end encrypted.
project.note: Decided means Hendrik decided it. Planned means agreed as a later step but not designed yet. Guess means a working assumption or a recommendation still waiting for a decision.

features.title: Sign-in without passwords
features.summary: Passkeys first, one-time email codes as the fallback, through Ory Kratos (open source). No passwords, no phone number, no custom auth code. Your account ID is a random code with no server name, bound to your phone's key. Recovering an account on a new phone waits 24 hours and tells the old phone, which can cancel it.

features.title: Profiles
features.summary: Photos, profile texts, interest tags and what you're looking for (stored as a list, one shown at first). You choose your own search groups, separate from your gender label; orientation is an optional label, hidden by default and never a filter. A new profile stays hidden until you publish it, and the publish step shows the privacy choices and asks for consent. Still open: how relationship types are described.

features.title: Discovery
features.summary: Search with filters and browse the results, OkCupid-style. No swiping, no card stack, no one-at-a-time decisions. Interest tags instead of free-text keywords; profile texts are searchable only for people who opt in. Previews show exact age, never the date of birth.

features.title: Opening messages
features.summary: Anyone can write one opening message per profile; the recipient's reply starts the conversation. 5 opening messages a week, 2 for new or unverified accounts, and the allowance comes back if a message expires unanswered after 30 days. Inboxes hold at most 15 unanswered messages (adjustable); senders then see a 'full' notice, never a number. No swiping and no mutual-like step. Future idea, not decided: an allowance relative to how many profiles fit your search.

features.title: Encrypted chat
features.summary: End-to-end encrypted with libsignal. The server only relays: it holds a message until it is delivered, then deletes it. A conversation starts once the recipient replies to an opening message.

features.title: Safety and verification
features.summary: Hide, block (silent, both ways, enforced by the server) and report (which always also blocks), with seven report reasons. CSAM and threats to life are handled immediately, under-18 reports within a few hours, the rest within 24 hours. Reported users hear about a report only if action is taken, with reasons and a way to appeal. Optional photo verification runs on the phone; only a signed yes or no reaches the server.

features.title: Deleting and exporting your data
features.summary: Deleting your account takes effect at once (after signing in again); backups expire after 30 days and photos are crypto-shredded. Inactive profiles are hidden after 3 months and deleted after 12, with warnings. Export by request during the test, in the app before real users. No IP logging in the test; later only keyed hashes, kept 7 days.

features.title: Coarse location
features.summary: No GPS. You pick your home tile on a Berlin map and choose how precisely it is stored: about 1.5 km by default, or 500 m, or district. Changing it is rate-limited. Results show travel time, not distance. A finer location is only shared phone to phone in a conversation.

features.title: Open source and portable
features.summary: Public repo, open code, no patents. In stage 2, anyone in the EU who signs the operator agreement can run a server that stores and relays encrypted data; servers that can read search data are run only by vetted operators.

mockups.title: Search
mockups.note: The design doc leaves list vs. grid open, and specifies a non-empty state for the early pilot -- shown as three options.

mockups.title: Write & save
mockups.note: Updated 11 Oct 2026: the design doc replaced mutual-liking with one opening message per profile, a reply starts the conversation, and a private Save/bookmark list. These mockups replace the earlier mutual-like ones.

mockups.title: Chat
mockups.note: A conversation opens once the recipient replies to an opening message (not a mutual like, which is no longer the model); the safety-controls layout isn't designed yet.

mockups.title: Profile
mockups.note: The design doc describes three distinct profile views (yours, theirs, and the preview card in results) -- none of these are final. The other-person view's actions are Write, Save, Hide, Block and Report, not Like.

architecture.summary: Two stages. The Berlin pilot runs on one server operated by an accountable legal entity, because search, blocking, bans and moderation need someone who can enforce rules and act as the GDPR controller. Later, one server program runs on two levels: sealed servers run by vetted operators, and plain servers that anyone in the EU can run under a signed agreement. The data model and the safety service are built so stage 2 doesn't need a rewrite.

stages.title: Stage 1: one server (Berlin pilot)
stages.summary: Phones talk to a single open-source server in Germany. It holds profiles, the search index (home tiles, never GPS), blocks, bans and the moderation queue. Chats are end-to-end encrypted; the server relays them and deletes each message once it is delivered.

stages.title: Stage 2: one program on two levels (later)
stages.summary: Every server runs the same program. The sealed level runs inside hardware enclaves that phones check before trusting them; it holds the small search cards and runs admission, ban and photo checks. Only vetted operators run it, in professional data centres, under a signed agreement. The plain level only stores and relays encrypted data (profile items, photos, messages); anyone in the EU who signs the operator agreement can run it. Profiles are no longer split into pieces across servers, and accounts belong to no home server. A shared ban list keeps a banned person out everywhere.

decisions.choice: One central open-source server
decisions.why: Search, blocking and moderation need an accountable operator; one shared pool helps the small pilot.
decisions.alternatives: Federation from day one, pure peer-to-peer

decisions.choice: Self-chosen home tile, stored at about 1.5 km by default (500 m or district selectable), no GPS, changes rate-limited
decisions.why: The stored precision is all an attacker can ever learn, so the default is a neighbourhood, not a few streets. Finer location only goes phone to phone in a conversation.
decisions.alternatives: GPS radius, 500 m default, district only

decisions.choice: Filtered search, no swiping
decisions.why: Better decisions, no dark patterns, no swipe-patent exposure.
decisions.alternatives: Card stack

decisions.choice: Ory Kratos with passkeys first, email codes as fallback; 24 h recovery wait with a cancel notice to the old phone
decisions.why: No passwords and no custom auth code to get wrong. The waiting period stops someone with access to the email inbox from silently taking over an account.
decisions.alternatives: Phone number, own auth

decisions.choice: Random opaque 128-bit ID, no @server, not derived from a key, bound to the device key by a certificate
decisions.why: Stable when a phone is lost, ties nobody to a server, and works with Kratos now and the stage 2 design later.
decisions.alternatives: id@server, hash of a phone key

decisions.choice: Interest tags (fixed list plus own short tags) and opt-in searchable profile texts: off by default, reciprocal, search words never logged; saved searches run on the phone
decisions.why: Free text for everyone would need readable texts on the server and would find labels people chose to hide.
decisions.alternatives: Free-text search over all profiles, no keyword search

decisions.choice: Age two-way with a 5-year margin; travel time one-way; a symbol on the tile when you're outside someone's range
decisions.why: Cuts unwanted messages without hiding people over small differences. Accepted leak: symbols hint where the other person's limits are.
decisions.alternatives: Age and travel time both two-way, only search groups two-way

decisions.choice: Self-chosen search groups separate from gender labels; orientation optional, hidden, never a filter; intentions stored as a list; exact age shown, never the date of birth; profile hidden until first published
decisions.why: Filters need as little Art. 9 data as possible, and nobody becomes visible before they have seen the privacy choices.
decisions.alternatives: Gender as the filter, orientation as a filter, age bands

decisions.choice: Optional on-device liveness and face comparison with its own consent; the server gets only a signed yes or no with app attestation
decisions.why: Scales without staff and keeps biometric data on the phone. The DPO and lawyer confirm the consent design before real users.
decisions.alternatives: Human check of a requested-pose photo, a vendor service

decisions.choice: libsignal E2EE + relay that deletes after delivery
decisions.why: Nothing readable or lasting on the server; works when the other phone is offline.
decisions.alternatives: Matrix (keeps history on servers), pure phone-to-phone (no offline delivery, leaks IPs)

decisions.choice: React Native + Expo, libsignal in our own native Kotlin/Swift module
decisions.alternatives: Flutter, Kotlin Multiplatform, fully native Kotlin + Swift
decisions.why: Fastest for one developer on both platforms; every option needs a native libsignal bridge anyway, and that module is reusable and fundable. See docs/design/app-framework.md.

decisions.choice: Berlin e.V., founded now with seven founders, before any public announcement or grant press
decisions.why: Someone has to be the GDPR controller and DSA hosting provider, and the project is already public, so liability should move off one person early.
decisions.alternatives: Found it only before real users, gGmbH, UG

decisions.choice: 5 opening messages a week (2 for accounts under two weeks old or unverified); allowance returned when a message expires unanswered after 30 days; inbox cap of 15 unanswered messages, adjustable, with a 'full' notice and no number
decisions.why: Limits mass messaging and overloaded inboxes without a hidden ranking; numbers are tuned with pilot data.
decisions.alternatives: No inbox cap, allowance never returned, allowance relative to available profiles (future idea)

decisions.choice: Seven report reasons; CSAM and threats to life immediately, under-18 within a few hours, the rest within 24 h; Hendrik plus one backup, both with escalation contacts
decisions.why: Clear targets for the worst cases and no single point of failure during the pilot. The backup is not named yet.
decisions.alternatives: Volunteer moderators, no fixed targets

decisions.choice: Instant deletion with a hold under open reports; 30-day backups with a replayed deletion list; photos crypto-shredded; only a ban record kept after a ban, 2 years; inactive accounts hidden at 3 months, deleted at 12
decisions.why: Smallest data set that still keeps bans effective. The lawyer confirms the 2-year period and the basis for the open-report hold.
decisions.alternatives: Delayed deletion with undo, keeping reports against non-banned accounts

decisions.choice: None during the fake-data test; before real users, keyed IP hashes (key rotated daily, kept 7 days) in the reverse proxy, Kratos, relay and safety service
decisions.why: Spots sign-up farms within a week without storing addresses that reveal where people are.
decisions.alternatives: Raw IPs for 7 days, no logging at all

decisions.choice: An EU-based transactional email provider with a DPA, minimal content, no app name in the subject if possible; provider not chosen yet (Scaleway, Lettermint or Brevo compared)
decisions.why: An email alone can reveal that someone uses a dating app, so it should say as little as possible and stay with an EU processor.
decisions.alternatives: A US email service, own mail server

decisions.choice: Self-declared date of birth for the fake-data test; the stronger check is chosen before real users (recommended: German eID age-only query, ID scan through an EU vendor as the fallback)
decisions.why: The DSA guidelines expect verification for high-risk services; the choice is deferred until real users are near.
decisions.alternatives: Selfie estimate only, human video check

decisions.choice: AGPL-3.0-or-later with a section 7 additional permission for app store distribution (LICENSE-EXCEPTION)
decisions.why: App store terms conflict with the AGPL; adding the permission is easy now while the copyright holders are few. The lawyer is asked once about libsignal on iOS.
decisions.alternatives: No exception, relicensing store builds

decisions.choice: Separate Hetzner CAX11 in Germany
decisions.why: Cheap, EU-hosted, isolated from other personal services.
decisions.alternatives: An existing personal server

decisions.choice: Bans, verification and hash lists in their own service with an API
decisions.why: Lets stage 2 share a blocklist between servers without a rewrite.
decisions.alternatives: Inside the main database

decisions.choice: One server program on two levels: sealed level run by vetted operators in data centres; plain level open to anyone in the EU who signs the operator agreement
decisions.why: Enclaves can be broken by someone with physical access, and every operator processes Art. 9 data, so the servers that read data need vetted, contracted operators. Storing and relaying ciphertext can be open to more people under the same agreement.
decisions.alternatives: Fully open servers, vetted servers only, server groups agreeing on state

decisions.choice: Profile content encrypted on the phone and stored on plain servers; only minimal search cards are readable, inside the sealed level
decisions.why: Plain operators only ever hold ciphertext, and an enclave break exposes little. Splitting profiles into k-of-n pieces is dropped: content is already encrypted, so it added a lot of work for little privacy.
decisions.alternatives: Encrypted pieces spread across servers (k-of-n), each server keeping its users' full profiles

open_questions: Stage 2: if the sealed level holds every profile's content key, an enclave break exposes full profiles. Accept that openly, or move to proxy re-encryption first?
Stage 2: where do sealed servers run (cloud confidential VMs or dedicated hardware)?
Does the open-source Kratos support passkeys in native apps? A one-day spike before building login.
Relationship type: what describes it beyond the intention (the 'intensity' question)?
Stage 2: which protocol between servers (ActivityPub, Matrix-style, or our own API)?
Stage 2: how does deleting an account reach other servers reliably (GDPR Art. 17(2)), and what must the operator agreement contain for each level?
Who runs the server and pays for it before the e.V. exists?
Which stronger age check before real users join: German eID age-only query, or an ID scan through an EU vendor?
Which EU transactional email provider for login codes (Scaleway, Lettermint, Brevo)?
Who is the named backup moderator for the pilot?

suggestions.intro: Recommendations from the research so far that still need a decision. Have an idea of your own? Open an issue on GitHub.

items.title: Apply to the Prototype Fund
items.summary: Pays developer time on public-interest open source (up to 47,500 € for one person). Current round closes 30 Nov 2026.

items.title: Apply to NLnet for one component
items.summary: For example the E2EE chat relay or libsignal bindings for React Native/Expo. Deadline 3 Nov 2026, noon CET.

items.title: Write down why phase 1 needs no DPO
items.summary: Holds only while phase 1 really uses fake data. A DPIA and an external DPO are needed once real dating data comes in.

items.title: Human security review before any real data
items.summary: Keep the pilot on test data until a person has reviewed the server, the relay and the sign-in setup.

items.title: Invite-only waves, balanced and recruited at events
items.summary: Gate waves so the gender and orientation mix stays balanced; open an area only once new users would see real profiles on day one.

items.title: Age check on the device
items.summary: Self-declared birthdate for the fake-data test. Before real users: on-device selfie age estimation, with the German eID age-only query (ID scan as fallback) for anyone near the line; the EU age-verification app once available. Never store ID scans.

items.title: Contact the Alovoa maintainer
items.summary: Report their encryption issue privately through their SECURITY.md and ask about sharing pieces later.

items.title: Register the name as a trademark
items.summary: German mark at the DPMA (around 290 €) before phase 2; consider an EU mark if stage 2 reaches other countries.
